title: A test that catches look-ahead
objectives: Write a test that fails if the engine ever peeks at the future.
Explain why a modest Sharpe proves nothing about look-ahead.

screens.title: Two ordinary curves
screens.prose: Two engines run the lookback-1 rule on `make_bars()`. Engine A holds 10,000 shares. Engine B sizes each position by $0.005 / \text{vol}$, where vol is `close.pct_change().std()`. Both report a Sharpe of 0.60. One of them uses the future.

state.caption: Same rule, same Sharpe of 0.60. B's positions are smaller.

screens.question: How could you tell which engine peeks?

options.text: Run each on the data up to a date and on all of it, and compare the rows before that date.
The one with the higher Sharpe peeks.
options.why: You looked for the leak in the result. Both Sharpes are 0.60, and a small leak can leave a Sharpe ordinary.

options.text: Neither peeks: both Sharpes are below 2.
options.why: You trusted a Sharpe below 2. That rule catches loud leaks only; a quiet one passes it.

options.text: Run both on a new seed and see which one fails.
options.why: You changed the data. A leaky engine runs happily on any seed; it just keeps peeking.

hints.text: Which engine's past would change if the future changed?
B's vol is computed over the whole series, including the years after each trade.
Cut the data: an honest engine's early rows cannot depend on rows that are not there.

feedback.correct: The curves cannot tell you; cutting the data can.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both results look the same, so the test must change the data, not read the result.

explain.text: B's vol uses every close in five years, so its size in 2019 depends on prices from 2023. Its Sharpe is the same because a constant scale does not change a Sharpe. Only a test that removes the future can see the difference.

screens.title: Cut and compare
screens.prose: Start with a loud leak. Engine C signs tomorrow's return: `np.sign(close.shift(-1) / close - 1)`. We run it on all of `make_bars()`, and on the first 600 rows, up to Tuesday 20 April 2021. The table shows the last five rows before the cut.
screens.question: Tap every row where the two runs disagree.

hints.text: Compare the target columns, then the shares columns.

feedback.correct: Only the last row before the cut disagrees, and only in its target.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two target columns and the two shares columns row by row.

byKey.r1: Thursday's targets agree: both runs saw Friday's close. Its shares agree too.

explain.text: On 20 April the full run reads 21 April's close and targets 10,000; the cut run has no 21 April, so it targets 0. The shares still agree, because that order would fill on 21 April, after the cut. The leak shows in the decision before it shows in the equity.

screens.title: The look-ahead check
screens.prose: What you just did is a **look-ahead check**: run the engine on the data before a cut and on all of it. An honest engine gives identical rows before the cut, since nothing there can depend on what comes after.
screens.question: A check that compared only shares, cash and equity would have missed engine C at this cut. Why?

options.text: The leaky target on 20 April fills at the next open, 21 April, after the cut.
The leak is too small to move equity.
options.why: You judged it by size. Engine C's Sharpe is 9.78; the leak is huge, it just shows up a row later.

options.text: The difference is lost in rounding.
options.why: You blamed rounding. The targets differ by 10,000 shares, not by a fraction.

options.text: The check should have used noise instead.
options.why: You switched tests. Noise after the cut would change the same row, and the shares would still agree.

hints.text: When does a target decided on 20 April become shares?
Orders fill at the next open (l5).
The shares move on 21 April, which the cut run never reaches.

feedback.correct: So the check compares every column the engine produces, the targets included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask on which row the 20 April target turns into shares.

explain.text: A decision on row $t$ becomes shares on row $t+1$. At the cut, that row is not there. So the check must compare the targets as well as the equity: every column, every row before the cut.

screens.title: Replace the future
screens.prose: A second form of the check keeps the rows after the cut but replaces their prices with seeded noise; the first rows must not move. Here is engine B, the full-sample vol, run on all the data and on the first 600 rows.
screens.question: Why does engine B disagree on every row, not just the last?

options.text: Its scale uses the vol of the whole series, so every day's size depends on the future.
It reads tomorrow's close, like engine C.
options.why: You took B for C. C changes only the last row; B uses one number from every row.

options.text: It charges costs differently in the two runs.
options.why: You looked at costs. Neither run charges any; the targets differ before any fill.

options.text: The cut run is wrong, not the engine.
options.why: You trusted the full run. The cut run sees only what was known then: it is the honest one.

hints.text: Compare 4,106 and 4,070 with the scale $0.005 / \text{vol}$.
Over five years vol is 1.218%; over the first 600 rows it is 1.228%.
Each target uses a vol computed from rows that include the future.

feedback.correct: One full-sample number reaches back into every row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the targets are scaled by.

explain.text: Five years give vol 1.218% and a size of 4,106; 600 rows give 1.228% and 4,070. Every target before the cut moved because the future moved. This is `validation` l10's scaling leak, in a backtest.

screens.title: The check in code
screens.prose: Now both forms in one function. `run(bars)` returns a DataFrame: one row per bar, columns `target`, `shares`, `cash` and `equity`. `noise_after(bars, cut)` is already defined: it scales every price after the cut by seeded noise from `np.random.default_rng(0)`. Compare to within 1e-9.
screens.question: Complete `lookahead_check`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on `make_bars(500)`: the honest engine with and without costs (True at cuts 100, 250 and 400), three planted leaks (False), a cut at the very last row, and an engine whose output is one row short. Compared with ==. `noise_after`, the engines and `make_bars` are already defined; the first run loads NumPy and pandas, 10 to 30 seconds.

hints.text: Three runs: all the data, the data before the cut, and the noisy data.
`part = run(bars.iloc[:cut])` and `noisy = run(noise_after(bars, cut)).iloc[:cut]`.
`same` is `a.shape == b.shape and np.allclose(a.to_numpy(float), b.to_numpy(float), rtol=0, atol=1e-9)`.

feedback.correct: True for the honest engines, False for every leak.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing case: it names the engine your check misjudged.

byKey.test-1: The honest engine failed your check. Compare only the first `cut` rows of each run.
byKey.test-2: Engine C passed. Compare every column, the targets included.
byKey.test-3: Engine B passed. Compare every row before the cut, to within 1e-9.
byKey.test-7: An engine with a row missing passed. Check that the shapes match before the values.

explain.text: `rtol=0` makes the tolerance absolute: 1e-9 of a share or a pound. The shape check stops a short output passing by accident. The noisy run catches leaks that only show when the future changes, not when it vanishes.

screens.title: Where to cut
screens.prose: A colleague's test runs the check once per engine, with `cut = len(bars)`. It passes on all three, engine C included.
screens.question: Why did engine C pass?

options.text: With nothing after the cut, both runs see the same data, so even a leak agrees.
Engine C was fixed since the last screen.
options.why: You assumed the engine changed. It did not; the test cannot see it at this cut.

options.text: The noise was too weak to matter.
options.why: You blamed the noise. At `len(bars)` there are no rows after the cut to replace.

options.text: It got lucky with the seed.
options.why: You blamed chance. At the last row, any engine passes every time.

hints.text: What is after the cut when `cut = len(bars)`?
Nothing, so the cut run and the full run read the same frame.
Cut in the middle, at several places.

feedback.correct: A cut at either end proves nothing; cut in the middle, more than once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each run can see when the cut is at the end.

explain.text: At the last row nothing is hidden, and at the first nothing is compared. Both pass trivially. Cut at several points in the middle, so a leak that starts late is still caught.

screens.title: A test that reads the Sharpe
screens.prose: Another colleague guards against look-ahead with a test that the Sharpe is below 2, the course's rule. It passes on engine B.
screens.question: What does the pass tell you about engine B?

options.text: Nothing about look-ahead: B leaks yet reports an ordinary 0.60.
B has no look-ahead, because its Sharpe is below 2.
options.why: You read a modest Sharpe as proof of honesty. B's leak only rescales its positions, so its Sharpe barely moves.

options.text: B leaks, but too little to matter.
options.why: You judged the leak by its effect today. On real data a full-sample scale can hide a regime the strategy never survived.

options.text: The bar should be 1 instead of 2.
options.why: You tightened the threshold. A leak can produce any Sharpe; no threshold separates them.

hints.text: What Sharpe did engine B report on the first screen?
0.60, the same as the honest engine.
A Sharpe test can flag a loud leak, never prove there is none.

feedback.correct: A Sharpe test catches loud leaks only; the cut test catches the quiet ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall engine B's Sharpe.

byKey.clean: You read a Sharpe below 2 as proof of honesty. B leaks and still reports 0.60.
byKey.small: You judged the leak by today's effect. A test must say whether the engine reads the future, not how much it gained.
byKey.raise: You tightened the threshold. A leak can give any Sharpe, so no threshold proves its absence.

explain.text: Engine B's leak changes its size, not its direction, so its Sharpe stays at 0.60. A threshold test catches engine C's 9.78 but not this. Look-ahead is a property of how the engine reads data, so the test must change the data.

screens.title: A test that fails on leaks
screens.prose: Put the check in the project's `tests/` folder. Write two pytest tests that call `lookahead_check` at several cuts in the middle of `make_bars(400)`. The hidden checks swap leaky engines in for `engine` and `engine_with_costs`; your tests must fail on each and pass on the honest ones.
screens.question: Write `test_engine_does_not_peek` and `test_engine_with_costs_does_not_peek`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. The first runs your tests on the honest engines: they must pass. Tests 2 to 6 swap a leaky engine in for `engine` or `engine_with_costs`: your tests must fail on each. Run examples runs pytest on your file and prints its report. pytest, NumPy and pandas load on the first run, 10 to 40 seconds.

hints.text: Each test is a loop over cuts with one `assert` inside.
Use the module's names `engine` and `engine_with_costs`, so the hidden checks can swap them.
`for cut in (100, 200, 300): assert lookahead_check(engine, bars, cut)`.

feedback.correct: Your tests pass on the honest engines and fail on all five leaks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing check: it names the engine your tests let through.

byKey.test-1: Your tests fail on the honest engines. Check the cuts are inside the data.
byKey.test-2: Engine C passed your tests. Use cuts in the middle of the data, not at its ends.
byKey.test-3: Engine B passed your tests. Call `lookahead_check`, which compares every row.
byKey.test-5: A leaky engine with costs passed. Your second test should check `engine_with_costs`.
byKey.test-7: Write both test functions, each named `test_...`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped before the tests ran. Read the error below the editor.

explain.text: Using the names `engine` and `engine_with_costs` makes the tests about the engine, not about one function. Several middle cuts catch leaks that start late. Every future change to the engine now has to pass them.

screens.title: One property
screens.prose:
Both forms test one property. Write the engine as a function $f$ of the bars $x_1, \dots, x_n$, giving rows $y_1, \dots, y_n$. For every cut $c$ with $1 < c < n$:
$$f(x_{1:c}) = f(x_{1:n})_{1:c} \quad \text{and} \quad f(x_{1:c}, \tilde{x}_{c+1:n})_{1:c} = f(x_{1:n})_{1:c}.$$
Here $\tilde x$ is any replacement future.
screens.question: A fourth engine fills at the close of the signal bar instead of the next open. Does the check fail it?

options.text: No: it reads only rows up to $t$, so it passes, though its fills are still too good.
Yes: a same-close fill is look-ahead, so the check fails it.
options.why: You expected the check to catch every timing error. This one uses no future rows; l5's fill rule, not this test, guards against it.

options.text: Only at some cuts.
options.why: You treated it as a late leak. It reads nothing after row $t$ at any cut.

feedback.correct: The check proves no future rows are read, and nothing more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does a same-close fill read any row after $t$?

explain.text: The property is about which rows a decision reads. A fill at the signal's close reads row $t$ only, so it passes, yet no real order gets that price. So the engine needs both l5's fill rule and this test.

screens.title: In the repository
screens.prose: In the project repository the two tests live in `tests/test_lookahead.py` and run on every push (`pytest` l12). A reviewer will not merge a change that breaks them (`git` l10). In an interview you are asked: how do you know your backtest has no look-ahead?
screens.question: Which answer is honest and complete?

options.text: A test cuts the data at several dates, and replaces the future with noise; the earlier output never moves. It runs on every push.
Its Sharpe is below 2, so it cannot be peeking.
options.why: You offered the Sharpe as proof. Engine B leaked at 0.60.

options.text: I was careful to use `shift(1)` everywhere.
options.why: You offered care instead of a test. One missed shift is a typo away, which is why the check exists.

options.text: It is impossible to know.
options.why: You gave up too soon. You cannot prove every bug absent, but this property you can test directly.

hints.text: What would convince a sceptic who has not read your code?
A test that changes the future and shows the past does not move.
Name the test, how it cuts, and when it runs.

feedback.correct: Evidence a reviewer can rerun, not a promise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the answer a sceptic could check for themselves.

explain.text: The honest answer names a test anyone can rerun. It says what it does not cover: the fill price and the costs, which have their own tests. Interviewers ask this to see whether you have been burnt before.

ideas: Cut the data: an honest engine's rows before the cut are identical whether or not the later rows exist, or are replaced by noise.
Compare every column, the decisions included: a leak at the cut shows in the target a row before it reaches the equity. Cut in the middle, several times.
A Sharpe below 2 proves nothing: a full-sample scaling leak reports an ordinary 0.60. The check runs in `tests/` on every push.

formula.name: No look-ahead
formula.note: And the same with the rows after $c$ replaced by noise.

summary.trap: Testing that the Sharpe is not too high. A quiet leak, such as a full-sample volatility, leaves the Sharpe ordinary.

quiz.prose: An engine fills at the next open. Its signal on row $t$ reads the close of row $t + 1$.
quiz.question: At a cut $c$, which column of row $c - 1$ shows the leak?

options.text: The target
The equity
options.why: You looked at the result. The order from row $c - 1$ fills on row $c$, after the cut.

options.text: None: the leak is invisible
options.why: You missed the decision column. The target on row $c - 1$ differs between the runs.

feedback.correct: The decision differs; the fill is after the cut.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which column is decided on row $c - 1$ itself?

explain.text: The target on row $c - 1$ reads row $c$, which the cut run lacks. Its fill lands on row $c$, outside the comparison, so only the target shows it.

quiz.question: Which does the look-ahead check catch? Select all that apply.

options.text: A signal from `close.shift(-1)`
A signal from `rolling(5, center=True).mean()`
Costs added to cash instead of taken off
options.why: You treated a cost bug as look-ahead. It reads no future rows, so the check passes it.

options.text: Fills at the close of the signal bar
options.why: You treated a bad fill as look-ahead. It reads only row $t$, so the check passes it.

feedback.correct: The check catches reads of future rows, and only those.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which bugs read a row after $t$.

explain.text: A shifted or centred window reads rows after $t$, so cutting the data changes earlier rows. A wrong cost sign or a same-close fill reads nothing later; other tests must catch them.

options.text: Nothing: it compares no rows
Every leak, since every row is after the cut
options.why: You counted the rows after the cut. The check compares the rows before it, and there are none.

options.text: Leaks in the first row only
options.why: With `cut = 0`, even the first row is outside the comparison.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many rows lie before the cut?

explain.text: With the cut at 0 there are no rows to compare, so it always passes. Cuts belong in the middle of the data.
